target_customer: Tech companies and their non-engineering teams that want internal tools and dashboards without engineering help
problem: Teams had business data spread across many apps and no easy way to combine it into one customizable board or internal tool.
business_model: SaaS with free tier and $10 per seat per month for advanced features

founders.name: Calum Moore
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch says he built Snapboard after a personal challenge to build one product a week for a year. He later worked on Polybase, a web3 database (YC page).

exit.reason: Site states the team is no longer working on Snapboard; no reason given.

competitors.name: Airtable
competitors.what: Spreadsheet-database no-code platform the founder used as the comparison ('Airtable, but with all of your data already in there')

technical_complexity.rationale: Connecting many app APIs into configurable boards is mostly integration work that a solo developer shipped, with no deep technical barrier.

defensibility.rationale: Integrations and dashboard UI were easy to copy, and the company had about 230 weekly active users at the time.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows a copy or acquisition; the product was later archived by its team.

market_need_then: TechCrunch reported about 3,000 registered users and around 230 weekly active users in March 2020, with a paid seat plan, which shows early interest but small engagement.

identity.voice_and_tone: Product pitched with a simple comparison to Airtable.

branding.community_and_virality: A Product Hunt listing named Snapboard (editable, hackable free dashboard, July 2019) ranked daily #1 per snippet, but I could not confirm the maker is the same.

brand_strength.rationale: One TechCrunch article and a Product Hunt listing of uncertain ownership; name resembles several other Snapboard and Smashboard products.

outcome_analysis: Snapboard was a solo-founder no-code dashboard and internal tools product from Winter 2020 with about 3,000 registered users and 230 weekly actives at launch. The company page now says the team stopped working on it and moved to other products, but no cause is stated, so failure factors are left empty. The thin engagement, low defensibility and a crowded no-code market are plausible contributors, but no source says so.
notes: Funding rests on TechCrunch (March 10, 2020), which states $150K from YC; CB Insights lists a $0.15M seed dated 2020-03-17 (single database, not opened). The amount is the standard YC deal and no other investors were found. A site fetch showed an archived page saying the team now builds Bookfolio and Mokly. Shutdown date not stated. CB Insights lists Mountain View, YC lists London. Retool and similar tools existed but no source dated to the batch was found, so they are not listed.
